extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent drafters, patent attorneys, and patent examiners in the Philippines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and prosecuting patent applications in the Philippines, covering substantive patentability standards (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability), formal application contents, specification/claim/drawing requirements, filing procedures, and examiner/practitioner considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are only valid in the country or region in which they have been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection is territorial — obtain protection in each jurisdiction where rights are desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant who files first will get the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority of rights is given to the first person to file an application for the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure (Quid pro quo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete; protection in exchange for disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant must provide sufficient disclosure so the public can carry out the invention after the patent expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional grant of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted only upon compliance with the criteria of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant depends on satisfying substantive and formal requirements (e.g., novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, sufficiency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is an exclusive right (for 20 years) granted for an invention, which is a product or a process that provides a new way of doing something or offers a new technical solution to a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To get a patent, technical information about the invention must be disclosed to the public in a patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Product examples: machine, device, article of manufacture, composition of matter, microorganism. Process examples: method of use, method of manufacturing, non-biological process, microbiological process. Computer-related inventions: inventions involving a computer, network or programmable apparatus with features realized wholly or partly by a computer program. Improvements to the foregoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-related inventions may be patentable if they involve technical features realized by computer/programmable apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable inventions (Sec. 22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes: (1) Discoveries; (2) Scientific theories; (3) Mathematical methods; (4) Schemes, rules and methods of performing mental acts, playing games, doing business, programs for computers; (5) Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy & diagnostic methods; (6) Plant varieties or animal breeds or essentially biological processes for production of plants/animals; (7) Aesthetic creations; (8) Anything contrary to public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are excluded from patent protection under the IP Code and relevant IRR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for patentability (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive requirements: (1) Novelty, (2) Inventive step, (3) Industrial applicability. Formal requirements: (a) Patentable subject matter, (b) Sufficiency of disclosure/enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application must satisfy both substantive and formal requirements to be granted a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (Sec. 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention shall not be considered new if it forms part of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty by comparison with prior art published or made available to the public before the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything made available to the public by means such as publications or internet publication constitutes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art sources include patent and non-patent literature, internet disclosures, public demonstrations, sales, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period / Non-prejudicial disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor disclosed or published the invention, demonstrated, sold or discussed it publicly, one can still file a patent within one (1) year from the date of disclosure or publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philippine law provides a one-year grace period for the inventor's own disclosures; document dates carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of novelty — single prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one prior art document/disclosure is to be considered for novelty; combination of separate items of prior art document/disclosure is not permissible for novelty assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For novelty, do not combine multiple prior disclosures — combination is an obviousness (inventive step) issue, not a novelty issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs Specific disclosure (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure does not take away the novelty of any specific example falling within the terms of that disclosure; a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims carefully: specific prior disclosures can anticipate broader generic claims; generic prior art may not anticipate specific embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents — novel vs obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ an equivalent to what is disclosed would be a matter of obviousness, not a question of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent substitutions are assessed under inventive step (obviousness) rather than novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / Non-obviousness (Sec. 26)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to prior art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the time of filing or priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is judged from the perspective of a person skilled in the art and considers motivation to combine, substitute or modify prior art with a reasonable likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'obvious' in patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention is obvious if the person skilled in the art would have been motivated or prompted to realize the claimed invention by substituting, combining, or modifying one or more items of prior art with a reasonable likelihood of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to 'lacking an inventive step'. Focus on motivation and reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (legal fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fictional person with no inventive ability, aware of common general knowledge in the specific art, having access to everything disclosed as the state of the art, and able to observe developments in related technical fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess what such a person would do when faced with the technical problem to be solved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of inventive step — Problem-Solution Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps: identify technical features of invention & prior art documents; determine the closest prior art; evaluate differences (distinguishing features); identify the technical problem to be solved; analyze whether the technical solution represents an unexpected or non-obvious advance over the closest prior art (consider combination with a second prior art reference or common general knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision involves answering: what would a person skilled in the art do when faced with the objective technical problem and aware of the state of the art?

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (Sec. 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that can be produced and used in any industry shall be industrially applicable; should have practical and real-life benefit in any field of human endeavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The invention must be capable of industrial application — mere theoretical or speculative inventions may fail this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Points to consider in drafting the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify: conduct patent search; enlist problems in prior art; what problem is sought to be solved; is it patentable subject matter; what is novel; is the solution obvious; has publication ensued; decide area and nature of protection (Domestic application, Paris Convention, PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the search and problem analysis to define scope of claims and filing strategy (domestic vs foreign, priority routes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Databases for prior art search (guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent databases (free): IPOPHIL online services, Google Patents, Espacenet, USPTO. Non-patent databases: Google Scholar, PubMed, scientific journals. Proprietary: CAS STN, EPOQUEnet, WIPS, IEEE, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search both patent and non-patent literature using multiple databases to establish novelty and inventive step context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application contents (Rule 404) and fees (Rule 401)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application shall contain: (a) a duly accomplished request for the grant of patent; (b) a description of the invention; (c) one or more claims; (d) drawings if necessary; (e) an abstract. Fees should be paid within one (1) month from the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all required parts are included at filing and fees paid timely to avoid formal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and description / Enablement (Sec.35, Rule 405, Rule 406.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art. Enabling disclosure shall contain a clear and detailed description of at least one way of doing the invention using working examples; contain sufficient and clear disclosure of the technical manner or process of making, performing, and using the same, leaving nothing to conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide working examples and sufficient technical detail so the invention can be practiced without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of the disclosure (Rule 919) — new matter prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: No deletion or addition shall broaden the disclosure of an application to include new matter after the filing date of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any post-filing amendments cannot introduce subject matter extending beyond the original disclosure; limit claim amendments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of the description (Rule 407)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description should include: Title; Technical Field; Background Art; Summary (Abstract of the Disclosure); Brief description of the several views of the drawings; Detailed Description; Claims; Abstracts; Drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the description to support claims and meet formal IRR requirements; include clear background and summary to contextualize inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirements (Rules 413-414)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing must be signed by the applicant or his attorney/agent; must show every feature of the invention; figures must be consecutively numbered; elements must be designated by reference numerals corresponding to the elements in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure drawings are clear, complete, signed, numbered and that reference numerals in drawings match the description for consistent claim support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — scope and quality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the scope/boundary of protection. Claims must be: (a) Clear (clarity) — avoid vague terms such as 'thin', 'strong', 'a major part', 'such as', 'when required'; (b) Complete (enablement) — cover the inventive feature and sufficient surrounding elements; (c) Supported (support) — all claim characteristics must be fully explained in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft clear, concise claims with adequate support in the description; avoid ambiguous wording and ensure claims are enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Entity claims: apparatus/device/product claims. Activity claims: method claims covering operations comprising one or more steps (e.g., manufacturing process, chemical process, software operation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select claim category appropriate to the invention (product vs method) and draft elements accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of claims — Independent and Dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claim: broadly describes the invention, typically written with broad terms, stands on its own (usually Claim 1). Dependent claim: describes the invention in a narrower aspect, clarifies independent claim language, expresses particular embodiments as fallback positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a broad independent claim plus dependent claims to provide fallback positions and to capture preferred embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a claim (preamble, body, transition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble: name of the subject matter or prior art environment. Body: recital of elements (structures, steps, parts or ingredients) and the manner in which elements cooperate. Transition: links preamble and body, often 'comprising' or 'which comprises' and typically followed by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claims with a clear preamble, properly recited elements in the body, and an appropriate transitional phrase; use consistent punctuation and grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural person, juridical person (a body of persons, corporation, partnership, or other legal entity recognized by law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entities recognized by law may be applicants; ensure correct applicant identity and representation at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and modes of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Philippine patent applications must be presented in either Filipino or English. Modes of filing: manual filing, through mails, online e-filing (www.ipophil.gov.ph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File in English or Filipino and consider e-filing for convenience; confirm procedural filing requirements on IPOPHL portal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of the patent holder
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner has the right to decide who may or may not use the patented invention during the protection period; patent owners may license or sell their rights; once a patent expires, the invention enters the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees can enforce exclusivity, license or assign rights; understand term (20 years from filing) and consequences of expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing routes and priority (Direct, Paris, PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct (national filing), Paris Convention route (with priority claim — 12 months), PCT route (international application, international publication by WIPO, national phase entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide filing strategy (domestic vs Paris vs PCT) based on desired foreign protection and timing of priority claims; observe PCT timelines for international phase and national entry.
